summary: A DHCPv4 server is the authoritative source of the IP addresses it has handed out. Leasequery gives other processes and devices a lightweight way to ask the server about that address information. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: DHCP Leasequery lets a relay agent ask a DHCP server for information about a client or address. The answer can help the relay restore network-location details it lost.

questions: how to query a dhcp server for lease information
how does a relay agent find a client location
subtitle: How a DHCP relay agent can ask a server who holds an address and where that client connects.

tldr.problem: A DHCP relay agent may learn where clients connect by inspecting DHCP messages, but it can lose that information after a restart or replacement.
tldr.mechanism: DHCPLEASEQUERY lets a relay agent ask a DHCP server about an IP address, hardware address, or Client-identifier. The server reports an active, unassigned, or unknown result.
tldr.outcome: The relay can rebuild location information from the DHCP server, which is authoritative for its leases. RFC 4388 is updated by RFC 6148.

today: RFC 4388 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2006 and is updated by RFC 6148.

sections.title: Recovering Client Location Information
sections.content:
A DHCPv4 server keeps authoritative information about the addresses it leases. A broadband access concentrator acting as a DHCP relay agent may need that information to associate an IP address with a client, port, virtual circuit, or modem.

The relay normally gleans details from DHCP messages it forwards, but it may lose them after reboot or replacement. DHCPLEASEQUERY lets it ask the server directly. The query does not change the address lease or binding.
sections.plainLanguage: A relay agent may lose its record of which client is connected to an address. Leasequery lets it ask the DHCP server that issued the address.

sections.title: Why Query the DHCP Server
sections.content:
The RFC considers using ARP broadcasts, SNMP, or LDAP to recover location information. ARP would send traffic across multiple ports and make subscriber hosts process broadcasts; a malicious host could also impersonate the endpoint. Access concentrators may not have SNMP or LDAP client interfaces.

DHCP servers participate in lease transactions and are therefore a reliable source of lease information. A relay can query the same servers it already uses, and can be configured with more than one server.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking the DHCP server avoids broadcasting a query to every host on the access network. The server already holds the lease information the relay needs.

sections.title: Three Ways to Identify a Client
sections.content:
A DHCPLEASEQUERY can identify an address by IP address, MAC address, or Client-identifier option. Querying by IP address asks for the most recent client assigned that address and SHOULD be used when possible. A MAC-address or Client-identifier query asks for an address most recently used by that client and may reveal other associated addresses.

A server that supports DHCPLEASEQUERY MUST implement all three query forms and answer queries. A server that does not support it SHOULD remain silent. Queries use the existing DHCP message format.
sections.plainLanguage: The relay can search by IP address, hardware address, or client identifier. The server's reply depends on which identifier the query supplied.

sections.title: Query Types and New Options
sections.content:
DHCP message type values 10 through 13 identify DHCPLEASEQUERY, DHCPLEASEUNASSIGNED, DHCPLEASEUNKNOWN, and DHCPLEASEACTIVE. The protocol also defines option 91, client-last-transaction-time, and option 92, associated-ip.

Option 91 reports how many seconds ago the client last interacted with the server about the address; it is a duration, not an absolute timestamp. Option 92 lists other IP addresses associated with the client and has a length that is a multiple of four octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Four DHCP message types identify a query and its possible answers. Two options add the time of the last client transaction and the client's other associated addresses.

sections.title: Server Answers and Retry Behavior
sections.content:
DHCPLEASEACTIVE means an active lease exists and can include the client's hardware address and requested options. DHCPLEASEUNASSIGNED means the server manages the address but there is no active lease. DHCPLEASEUNKNOWN means the server lacks definitive information; that response must not include other DHCP options.

The relay should cache unassigned results and cache unknown results for a short time, approximately five minutes. If no response arrives, it cannot know whether the query was lost or the server does not support leasequery. The RFC recommends exponential backoff and limits parallel queries to 100 or 200.
sections.plainLanguage: The server says whether the address has an active lease, is managed but unassigned, or is unknown. The relay caches answers and waits longer between repeated queries when a server is silent.

messages.label: DHCPLEASEQUERY
messages.note: Requests information about an address or client.

messages.label: DHCPLEASEACTIVE
messages.note: Reports an active lease and related information.
